units.t: Maths Shorts.
In this episode: Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding and Calculus without fear: the maths of change.
Part one. Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding.
In 1614 a Scottish nobleman published tables that saved astronomers years of drudgery.
For the next 350 years, his idea sat in the pocket of every engineer as the slide rule.
The drudgery of multiplying.
Picture an astronomer around 1600 working out a planet's orbit.
Each step means multiplying and dividing numbers of seven or more digits, and one slip ruins weeks of work.
Navigators and surveyors faced the same burden.
Adding large numbers is quick and fairly safe, but multiplying by hand means rows of partial products and lots of carrying.
Mathematicians wondered whether hard multiplication could become easy addition.
A clue came from powers.
Since 2 times 2 times 2 is 8 and 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 is 16, multiplying 8 by 16 means adding the counts of twos, 3 plus 4, to get 7 twos.
That is 128.
Napier's idea.
John Napier was the Laird of Merchiston near Edinburgh, who also wrote a fiercely argued book on the Book of Revelation.
Mathematics was his passion.
He spent around two decades developing logarithms, a word built from Greek roots meaning ratio and number, and published them in 1614.
His tables paired numbers with their logarithms.
Napier's version differs from today's, but the essential trick was there.
With base 10, the logarithm of 100 is 2 and of 1,000 is 3.
The logarithm of 2 is about 0.
301 and of 8 about 0.
Add them to get 1.
204, look up the number with that logarithm, and you find 16, which is 2 times 8.
Division becomes subtraction, powers become multiplication, and square roots become halving.
Briggs and Kepler.
The English mathematician Henry Briggs travelled to Scotland in 1615 to meet Napier.
They agreed that logarithms would be more convenient in base 10, so the logarithm of 10 was 1 and of 100 was 2.
Napier died in 1617.
Briggs calculated the new tables by hand, including a large volume in 1624.
These common logarithms stayed in classrooms, including Australian ones, until cheap electronic calculators arrived in the 1970s.
The astronomer Johannes Kepler seized on logarithms early.
He used them in completing the Rudolphine Tables, published in 1627, which predicted planetary positions far more accurately than anything before.
Logarithms did not create the scientific revolution, but they made its endless calculations bearable.
The slide rule.
Soon after Napier, the English mathematician Edmund Gunter drew a ruler marked with a logarithmic scale, so distances along it represented logarithms.
Using dividers, users could add lengths and so multiply numbers.
In the 1620s and 1630s the clergyman William Oughtred slid two such scales against each other, which did the adding automatically.
This was the slide rule.
For centuries it was the engineer's constant companion, helping design bridges, ships, aircraft and, at NASA, the rockets of the Apollo programme.
A good slide rule gave about three significant figures, accurate enough for most engineering.
Pocket calculators replaced it almost overnight in the 1970s.
Logarithms today.
Calculators made log tables obsolete, but logarithms are everywhere.
The decibel scale for sound is logarithmic: every 10 decibels means ten times the sound intensity.
Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic, as is the pH scale, where each step is a tenfold change.
In finance and biology, logarithms describe compound growth and halving.
Your senses seem to work roughly logarithmically too, noticing proportional changes rather than absolute ones.
An extra candle brightens a dark room far more than a sunny one.
The idea Napier spent twenty years refining still shapes how scientists see the world, long after its original purpose disappeared.
The key idea: Adding is easy and multiplying is hard, and patterns in powers hint at a way to turn one into the other.
Part two. Calculus without fear: the maths of change.
Calculus has a fearsome reputation, but its two big ideas can be grasped with a speedometer and an odometer.
Its invention also sparked one of the bitterest feuds in science.
Two simple questions.
Strip away the symbols and calculus asks two questions.
How fast is something changing at this exact moment?
And if you know how fast it is changing, how much has it added up to over time?
Every car shows both ideas.
The speedometer reports how fast your distance is changing right now.
The odometer adds up all those changing speeds into a total distance.
The first idea is differentiation, which gives a derivative.
The second is integration, which gives an integral.
Together they sit at the heart of physics, engineering, economics and biology, anywhere things change smoothly.
Ordinary arithmetic copes with fixed values.
Calculus copes with constant change.
Ancient near-misses.
Long before anyone named calculus, the Greeks wrestled with its core difficulty.
Around the fifth century BCE, Zeno of Elea argued that swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise with a head start, since each time he reaches where it was, it has moved on.
How can infinitely many steps add up to a finite result?
Today we can answer: a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever totals exactly 1.
In the third century BCE, Archimedes squeezed a circle between polygons inside and outside it.
With 96 sides, he showed pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7, about 3.
He used similar reasoning for the area under a parabola and the volume of a sphere.
He lacked a general method.
Newton versus Leibniz.
In the mid-1660s, with Cambridge closed by plague, young Isaac Newton developed his method of fluxions but kept it largely to himself.
In Germany, Gottfried Leibniz developed his own version in the 1670s and published first, in 1684.
A bitter priority dispute followed, with Newton's supporters accusing Leibniz of plagiarism.
In 1712 the Royal Society, which Newton led as president, ruled in Newton's favour in a report he secretly drafted much of himself.
Historians now agree the two men invented calculus independently.
Leibniz's notation, such as dy/dx and the long S for an integral, proved clearer and won out.
British mathematicians, loyal to Newton's dots, fell behind continental Europe for decades.
Zooming and slicing.
Drop a ball and it falls about 4.
9 times t² metres in t seconds, ignoring air resistance.
How fast is it moving at exactly one second?
From 1 to 1.
1 seconds, the average speed is 10.
29 metres per second.
From 1 to 1.
01, it is about 9.
As the interval shrinks, the average closes in on exactly 9.
That limit is the derivative: the slope of a curve at a single point.
Integration runs the other way.
A steady 60 kilometres an hour for two hours is a rectangle on a speed graph, 60 high and 2 wide, so 120 kilometres.
For varying speed, slice the area into thin strips and add them up.
Infinitely thin strips give the exact answer.
Engineers use this for forces on dams and volumes of fuel tanks.
Why calculus took over.
The deepest discovery is that the two halves undo each other.
Integrate a speed to get distance, differentiate that, and you get the speed back.
This is the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher, had glimpsed it, but Newton and Leibniz made it a working method.
Instead of adding thousands of strips, you find a formula whose derivative matches your curve, and the area follows almost instantly.
Yet the foundations were shaky.
In 1734 George Berkeley mocked vanishing quantities as ‘ghosts of departed quantities’.
In the nineteenth century, Cauchy and Weierstrass rebuilt calculus on precisely defined limits, answering Zeno at last.
Today it underpins weather forecasts, rocket trajectories, medical scanners and AI training, which follows derivatives downhill to reduce errors.
The key idea: Calculus answers two questions: how fast something is changing right now, and how much has built up over time.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Using powers of 2, why does 8 times 16 equal 128?
Answer. Three twos and four twos make seven twos.
Question two. In the car picture of calculus, what does the odometer represent?
Answer. Adding up changing speeds into a total distance.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
